pages.text:
*Sky Report: light rain clearing, first sun on wet rock, a lot of exhausted birds.*

The Lantern Isles rose from the water like a spilled bucket of green jade, topped with tiny stone towers that glowed with a soft, steady amber light. The flock hit the rocks in a tangle of feathers and exhaustion. Birds landed in heaps, some sleeping instantly, others just standing with their eyes closed, wings drooping.

Gullet appeared. He was a seagull the size of a boulder, with feathers like snow and a beak like a rusty nail. He waddled through the crowd with surprising gentleness, his heavy feet padding on the wet stone. He held a fish head in his beak, offering it to a shivering wren.

"Here, you small thing," Gullet rumbled, his voice a low rumble. "Eat. It is cold out."

The wren took a bite. Then another.

Pip landed on a flat rock, her legs trembling so badly she could barely keep her balance. She looked at the glowing towers, then at the fish head being passed around. Her stomach gave a loud, hollow growl. She realized, with surprise, that she was very, very hungry.
pages.image: A tiny brown sparrow with a crooked tail stands on a wet rock among sleeping birds, while a giant friendly white seagull waddles nearby holding a fish head in his beak; low green islands with glowing amber lighthouses rise from the sea behind them.

pages.text:
Marra arrived last, her torn wing dragging across the wet stone as she led the ragged line of survivors. Their feathers were matted, their eyes dull with the kind of tiredness that goes deeper than sleep.

She saw Pip.

The small brown bird was buried in the center of a large heap of sleeping sparrows, her chest heaving against the soft down, her crooked tail feather sticking straight up like a stubborn antenna. Marra’s beak opened. It closed. She opened it again, but no words came out.

Instead, she sank down onto a jagged rock, her legs folding under her weight until she looked older than she ever had, her grey streaks fading into the heavy evening shadow.

A young sparrow, his feathers still ruffled from the storm, hopped closer to tell her what had happened. He spoke of the wind-lanes, the hawk, and the way Pip had lifted the flock, one by one, from the chaos. Marra listened with her eyes closed, her head tilted slightly to the side. She did not blink, holding on to the story as if it were a seed she was afraid to drop.
pages.image: A large grey-streaked sparrow with a torn wing tip sits slumped on a dark rock, eyes closed, listening to a small sparrow speak; a tiny brown sparrow with a crooked tail sits nestled in a pile of other sleeping birds nearby.

pages.text:
Dawn came in grey sheets, and the counting began. The Elders moved in pairs, their voices low and serious, calling out names. It was a solemn, quiet thing, the counting of the living.

"Thistlewick," said one Elder. "Fern. Present."

"Old Bramble. Present."

"Nine. Present."

Nettle was asleep on her feet, her head bobbing gently with every call. Pip stood beside her, keeping one eye on the crowd. Cinder was there, too. He looked terrible. His glossy chestnut feathers were dull, and he kept bowing to every bird that passed, murmuring apologies for things he had not done.

"Sorry," he whispered to a wren. "Sorry about the loop. I didn't mean to show off."

The wren blinked, confused, and preened.

Pip watched Cinder, and then she watched the sky. The numbers were ticking up. It felt like holding your breath.
pages.image: A group of sparrows on a rocky shore at dawn, with a large grey elder sparrow counting them off; a tiny brown sparrow stands alert next to a skinny freckled sparrow who is sleeping with her head bobbing, while a chestnut sparrow bows apologetically to a wren.

pages.text:
A shadow dropped over Pip’s feet, and she looked up. Uncle Dorn stood there, very stiff, his feathers bristling while his eyes remained bright and watery. He had not moved from the edge of the rocks, and he had been watching.

"I knew you could fly," he said, his voice tiny. "I have always known. I was afraid, and it is not your fault."

Pip’s heart gave a sharp, painful thud.

"I am not sorry I said it," Dorn continued, his gaze fixed on the horizon. "I am sorry I said it so many times."

He turned his face away, for old sparrows do that when they cry. They look at the water and pretend they are just watching the waves.

"Small birds go where they like," he whispered.

Pip stepped forward and pressed her small, warm body against his side, tucking her head under his wing. He did not grumble, nor did he say low was safe. He just stood there, trembling, as the first real sun of the day touched the wet stone.
pages.image: A plump, gloomy grey-brown sparrow stands stiffly on a rock, turning his face away, while a tiny brown sparrow with a crooked tail presses her head under his wing; the sun is just rising over the sea, casting a golden light on their feathers.

pages.text:
The final count came in. All but three were present. The Elders confirmed the last three were safe on the far shore, waiting for the tide to turn.

A long sigh rippled through the flock. It was not a word, but a sound that moved from bird to bird. It was the rustle of relief and exhaustion, filling the air like wind moving through dry leaves.

Pip looked at Nettle, who was awake now with wide, shining eyes. She looked at Cinder, who was finally standing up straight. Then she looked at Uncle Dorn. He was watching her with a new, strange softness that made her toes curl.

Then Marra stood up on the high rock.

The crowd went silent. The Elders stepped back. Young sparrows pressed close to their parents. Marra smoothed her torn wing. She looked at Pip. She looked at the sky, which was finally, fully blue.

"I have something to say," Marra said. Her voice was gravel and stone, but it was steady. "It will not be easy for me. Sit."
pages.image: A large grey-streaked sparrow with a torn wing stands on a high rock in golden morning light, looking out at a large crowd of sparrows; a tiny brown sparrow with a crooked tail sits in the crowd, looking up at her with bright eyes.
